questions.question: What job titles or levels are you targeting next (be specific: e.g. Staff Engineer, EM L5)?
questions.answer: Staff Engineer or principal IC on platform/reliability; open to small team lead without full-time people management.

questions.question: What three themes should a reader take away from your resume in the first 10 seconds?
questions.answer: Reliability at scale, cross-team execution, measurable customer and business impact.

questions.question: Exact job title(s) as you want them on the resume (include level if relevant).
questions.answer: Senior Software Engineer

questions.question: Employer name (and parent company if known/acquired).
questions.answer: Riverbank Payments (Series C fintech).

questions.question: Start date (month/year) and end date or "Present".
questions.answer: Mar 2021 – Present

questions.question: In plain language, what does the company do and who pays for it (B2B, B2C, internal)?
questions.answer: B2B payment orchestration and settlement APIs for marketplaces and SaaS; revenue from transaction fees and enterprise contracts.

questions.question: What was your team called, and where did it sit in the org chart (product line, platform, infra)?
questions.answer: Payments Core — reported under Platform Engineering; sibling teams for ledger and risk.

questions.question: Were you on-call? Describe rotation length, severity of pages, and ownership boundaries.
questions.answer: Weekly primary/secondary rotation; Sev1–2 for API errors and settlement delays; owned runbooks for refund pipeline.

questions.question: In 2–3 sentences, what were you hired to do?
questions.answer: Own reliability and incremental delivery for external payments APIs; work with product on refunds, disputes, and idempotency guarantees.

questions.question: In 2–3 sentences, what did you actually end up doing (often broader/narrower)?
questions.answer: Also drove observability standards, led one large Kafka→queue migration, mentored two mid-level engineers, and represented eng in quarterly planning.

questions.question: What did you own end-to-end (codebase, service, product area, process)?
questions.answer: Refund and adjustment service (Go), related async workers, SLOs, and incident response for that slice.

questions.question: List up to 10 measurable outcomes tied to your work (metric + before/after or absolute result).
questions.answer: p95 refund API 800ms→220ms; payment incidents 4/mo→<1/mo; saved ~$200k/yr AWS after rightsizing and deduping egress; MTTR for refund Sev2 down 35%.

questions.question: What was the business impact of your top 3 wins (revenue, cost, risk reduction, time-to-market)?
questions.answer: Fewer failed refunds reduced support load and churn risk; cost savings in infra; faster releases for compliance-driven changes.

questions.question: Project name (internal or customer-facing). [Project: Refund pipeline hardening]
questions.answer: Project Northstar — refund pipeline reliability and observability overhaul.

questions.question: Why did this project exist (problem statement)? [Project: Refund pipeline hardening]
questions.answer: Opaque failures and retries were causing duplicate credits and support escalations during peak load.

questions.question: List every technology materially used (languages, frameworks, infra, data stores, messaging). [Project: Refund pipeline hardening]
questions.answer: Go, gRPC, PostgreSQL, Kafka (later SQS), Redis, Kubernetes, Datadog, Terraform.

questions.question: For each major technology: what did it let you accomplish that would have been harder otherwise? [Project: Refund pipeline hardening]
questions.answer: Go+K8s for predictable deploys; PG for strong consistency on adjustments; Kafka then SQS for decoupled retry semantics; Datadog for trace-backed SLOs.

questions.question: Would you choose the same stack again for a similar problem—why or why not? [Project: Refund pipeline hardening]
questions.answer: Yes on Go/PG/K8s; would pick managed queue sooner (SQS) over self-managed Kafka for our scale and ops load.

questions.question: How did you approach observability (logs, metrics, traces, alerts)—what did you instrument?
questions.answer: RED metrics per endpoint, trace IDs through async jobs, SLO dashboards, paging only on user-visible error budget burn.

questions.question: Describe a time you aligned multiple teams toward a shared deadline.
questions.answer: Coordinated ledger, risk, and support for a regulatory reporting change; shared cutover checklist and daily 15m sync for two weeks.

questions.question: What might a skeptical interviewer doubt—what evidence addresses that doubt?
questions.answer: Might think I only did features — point to SLO ownership, incident reviews authored, and infra cost work with finance sign-off.

questions.question: If you could change one thing about this role or company while you were there, what would it be—and what does that say about what you value?
questions.answer: Earlier investment in load testing in staging; value proactive validation over heroics in prod.

questions.question: List tools, frameworks, and cloud services you can defend in interview (comma-separated or bullets).
questions.answer: Go, PostgreSQL, Kafka, SQS, Redis, Kubernetes, AWS (EKS, RDS), Terraform, Datadog, GitHub Actions.

questions.question: Paste a sample target job description (or bullet list) you care about—what matches strongly vs weakly?
questions.answer: Strong: distributed systems, payments, SLOs, on-call. Weaker: heavy ML pipeline ownership — adjacent only via analytics for experiments.
